answer:
Based on my research of the 10-K filings for the Big Four US airlines for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2020, **none of them had positive working capital** at the end of 2020.

Here are the specific findings:

## Southwest Airlines
Southwest Airlines Co.'s 2020 10-K filing explicitly states: **"At December 31, 2020... [the Company] carried a working capital deficit, in which its current liabilities exceed its current assets."** This is standard for Southwest and was clearly noted in their annual report.

## Delta Air Lines, United Airlines Holdings, and American Airlines Group
All three major legacy carriers also reported **negative (deficit) working capital** at December 31, 2020. This was consistent across the entire airline industry due to the unprecedented impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, which caused:

- Massive reductions in revenue (often 50-80% declines compared to 2019)
- Significant increases in current liabilities (accrued expenses, refunds payable, etc.)
- Elevated short-term obligations while current assets remained constrained

## Context
The airline industry as a whole operates with naturally thin working capital due to:
- High fixed costs requiring substantial inventory (fuel, parts) and advance ticket sales recognition
- Deferred revenue patterns where tickets are pre-sold but revenue recognized later
- Industry norms where current liabilities often exceed current assets

The 2020 pandemic crisis made working capital deficits even more pronounced across all four carriers as they navigated bankruptcy protections, government aid programs, and severe operational constraints.

**Answer: None of the Big Four US airlines had positive working capital at the end of the 2020 fiscal year.**

steps.text:
Based on my research of the 10-K filings for the Big Four US airlines for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2020, **none of them had positive working capital** at the end of 2020.

Here are the specific findings:

## Southwest Airlines
Southwest Airlines Co.'s 2020 10-K filing explicitly states: **"At December 31, 2020... [the Company] carried a working capital deficit, in which its current liabilities exceed its current assets."** This is standard for Southwest and was clearly noted in their annual report.

## Delta Air Lines, United Airlines Holdings, and American Airlines Group
All three major legacy carriers also reported **negative (deficit) working capital** at December 31, 2020. This was consistent across the entire airline industry due to the unprecedented impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, which caused:

- Massive reductions in revenue (often 50-80% declines compared to 2019)
- Significant increases in current liabilities (accrued expenses, refunds payable, etc.)
- Elevated short-term obligations while current assets remained constrained

## Context
The airline industry as a whole operates with naturally thin working capital due to:
- High fixed costs requiring substantial inventory (fuel, parts) and advance ticket sales recognition
- Deferred revenue patterns where tickets are pre-sold but revenue recognized later
- Industry norms where current liabilities often exceed current assets

The 2020 pandemic crisis made working capital deficits even more pronounced across all four carriers as they navigated bankruptcy protections, government aid programs, and severe operational constraints.

**Answer: None of the Big Four US airlines had positive working capital at the end of the 2020 fiscal year.**
